title: Writing Files and Reliable Reports
lede: Choose a text format, write complete records, close resources, and check what a later reader receives. Separate computation from presentation so reports can be tested without depending on a real file.

sections.title: Output is a data contract
concepts: Write the format down first

Some output is read by a person: a message on the screen, a table in a printed report. Some is read by another program: a file that a spreadsheet, a marking script or next month’s version of your own program will open. A person shrugs at a missing comma or an extra space. A program cannot. It splits, counts and converts exactly the characters it receives, so every detail of your output becomes a promise.

Write that promise down before you write the first line of output. For a file of marks, the format contract answers questions like these:

QuestionOne possible answer
What does one line hold?one student: name, then mark
Is there a header line?yes, exactly name,mark, first
What separates the fields?one comma, no spaces around it
How is a number written?digits only: 85, not 85.0 or 85 marks
Which encoding?UTF-8, so Nguyễn survives (Section 2)
How does each line end?one \n, after every record, the last one too
What does “no students” look like?the header line on its own

Then keep three jobs apart: calculate the values, format them into text, and send the text somewhere (the screen, a string in memory, a file). A method that does all three at once can only be tested by opening a file; a method that returns a formatted string can be tested with one println.

Display text is not a file format

Printing a list or an array gives text chosen for humans, and nobody promised to keep it the same. Python prints ['Linh', 85]; Java prints an int[] as [I@ followed by a hexadecimal number that changes from run to run. Neither is something another program should parse. Build each record yourself, field by field, in the order the contract says.

The right numbers in the wrong units, 1999

NASA’s Mars Climate Orbiter was lost on 23 September 1999. One ground program wrote thruster data into a file whose interface specification required metric units (newton-seconds); it wrote pound-force seconds instead. The navigation software read the file as the specification promised. The investigation board’s words: the specification, “which was not followed, defines both the format and units” of the file. The values came out low by a factor of 4.45, and after nine months of small errors the spacecraft arrived about 170 km lower than planned. Mishap Investigation Board, Phase I report (1999)

“Expect the output of every program to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program. Don’t clutter output with extraneous information.”

Doug McIlroy, with E. N. Pinson and B. A. Tague, foreword to the UNIX issue of the Bell System Technical Journal, 1978 Portrait: Denise Panyik-Dale, 2011 · CC BY 2.0
print, println and write

Java and Python give you the same three moves, under different names: write some text, write some text and end the line, or write a formatted value. The one that causes trouble is the first, because nothing visible happens until the next piece of text lands on the same line. Java’s print and Python’s write store exactly the characters you give them. Java’s println adds a line end; Python’s write never does, so " " is part of the text you pass.

What exactly is “a line end”? Java’s println writes the system line separator: on Linux and macOS, on Windows. Python writes , and a file opened in text mode on Windows turns each into as it saves (unless you open it with newline=""). Most readers accept both, but a contract should say which one it means. The Miscellaneous panel Two characters for one new line explains why there are two.

Every record needs its newline, the last one too

" ".join(records) puts newlines between records, not after the last one. Append another record later and it is glued onto the end of that last line; wc -l, which counts newline characters, reports one line fewer than you wrote. End each record as you write it: println, or write(record + " ").
The same three moves in both languages

The same moves, side by side. out is a PrintWriter in Java and an open text file or StringIO in Python.

You wantJava (PrintWriter, System.out)Python file or StringIOPython print

a numberout.print(85) converts itout.write(str(85)); write(85) is a TypeErrorprint(85) converts it

Python’s print is the friendly one: it converts values to text, puts sep (a space) between them and end (a newline) after them, and file=out sends all that to a file instead of the screen.
Reports for people: width, alignment, decimals

A report for people has a different contract: the columns must line up, and numbers need a sensible number of decimals. Both languages describe that with a small format specifier: a width (the minimum number of characters), an alignment, and for decimals the digits after the point. The interactive diagram A report for people: make the columns line up lets you try each one.

EffectJava printf / String.formatPython f-stringResult (| marks the edges)
text, left-aligned in 8%-8s{name:<8}|Linh    |
whole number, right-aligned in 5%5d{mark:>5}|   85|
one digit after the point%.1f{avg:.1f}|72.5|
width 6, one decimal%6.1f{avg:6.1f}|  72.5|
line end%n\n

A width never cuts a value: a name longer than 8 characters simply pushes the rest of its row to the right. Choose widths for the longest value you expect, and keep machine-readable files free of padding altogether: Linh,85, not Linh    ,   85.

In Java, the decimal point depends on the computer

String.format and printf follow the computer’s locale. With a Vietnamese locale, %.1f writes 72,5, with a decimal comma: right for a person in Vietnam, wrong for a CSV file where the comma separates fields. For files, pass Locale.ROOT: String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%.1f", avg). Python’s f-strings always use a point (only the n format type follows the locale). The example The locale can move the decimal point below shows the difference.

media.alt: A split-flap train departure board listing time, train number, destination, origin and status in fixed columns
media.lead: Everyone can read the board because the columns never move.
media.caption: Time, train number, destination, status: the same fields in the same order on every row, so a traveller (or a program) knows where to look without reading any instructions. That is a format: field order, separator and one record per line, agreed before anything is written. Where it breaks: a destination too long for its column has to be abbreviated, because the board has a fixed width. A text file has no columns, so it needs a delimiter instead, and the next sections show what happens when a value contains that delimiter.

media.alt: A printed till receipt from a Swiss mountain hotel bar listing four items, each on its own line, then the total in bold
media.lead: Every item gets its own line, because the printer ends each one.
media.caption: A till printer prints an item’s name and price, then feeds the paper to a new line before the next item. That is println: the text and the line ending. print and Python’s write print only the text, so if nobody adds the newline, the next item lands on the end of the same line, and a program reading the receipt back line by line sees one item where there were two.

RFC 4180, published in October 2005, opens by admitting that “there is no formal specification in existence, which allows for a wide variety of interpretations of CSV files.” It is only informational, not a standard, and it ends each record with CRLF: two characters, carriage return and line feed. sections.title: File modes, closing and error reporting
concepts: Overwrite and append are different promises

Opening a file for writing is a decision about what happens to the text already in it. Make that decision on purpose, before the program runs, because nothing warns you afterwards.

You wantPythonJava 8File already existsFile missing
replace the contentsopen(p, "w")new PrintWriter(p, "UTF-8")emptied at oncecreated
add at the endopen(p, "a")new FileWriter(p, true)kept; new text goes after itcreated
create, never replaceopen(p, "x")Files.newBufferedWriter(path, StandardOpenOption.CREATE_NEW)FileExistsError / FileAlreadyExistsExceptioncreated

Java’s FileWriter in Java 8 always uses the computer’s default encoding. To append in UTF-8, wrap new FileOutputStream(p, true) in an OutputStreamWriter with "UTF-8"; the true means append.

The file is emptied when you open it, not when you write

open(p, "w") and new PrintWriter(p) truncate the file the moment they open it. If the program then crashes, or has nothing to write, the old contents are already gone. The classic version of this bug opens the same file for reading and for writing at once: the reader finds an empty file. Read everything you need first, close it, then open the file for writing.
Close before checking the saved result

Writing to a disk is slow compared with writing to memory, so a writer collects your text in a buffer and sends it to the file in large batches. Text leaves the buffer in three ways: the buffer fills up, you call flush(), or you call close(), which flushes and then releases the file. Until then, another program, or your own program reading the file back, may see an empty or incomplete file. That is the post box in the photo: posted is not delivered.

Closing proves that the writer has finished; it does not prove the data was right. Only reading the file back, with the reader you intend to use, tells you what a later program will receive.

A program that never closes can leave an empty file

In Java, text still in a PrintWriter’s buffer when the program ends is lost: the file can be empty or cut off in the middle of a line. Python usually flushes open files when a program ends normally, but not when it is killed or crashes hard. Do not rely on either: use try-with-resources and with.
Let the language close it: try-with-resources and with

You will forget to call close() one day, or an exception will jump over it. So both languages can close for you when a block ends, however it ends:

When writing fails: exceptions and checkError

Writing can fail: the folder does not exist, you have no permission, the disk is full, the USB stick was pulled out. The two languages report failures differently, and Java’s PrintWriter is the odd one out.

What goes wrongJavaPython
the folder does not existnew PrintWriter("no/such/dir/r.txt") throws FileNotFoundException, a checked IOExceptionopen(…, "w") raises FileNotFoundError, a kind of OSError
no permissionalso FileNotFoundException, with “Permission denied” in the messagePermissionError
a later write fails (disk full)BufferedWriter.write throws IOException; PrintWriter.println throws nothing and sets an error flagwrite, flush or close raises OSError

Because println on a PrintWriter never throws, a program can finish happily having saved nothing. When the result matters, call checkError() before you report success: it flushes the stream and returns true if any write has failed. The Java file example below does exactly that, and turns the flag into an IOException that a caller cannot ignore.

Don’t print “Saved!” from a catch-all

catch (Exception e) { } and except: pass turn a failed save into a silent one, which is worse than a crash: the user walks away believing the report exists. Catch the specific exception, tell the user what failed and where, or let it travel up to a caller that can decide (Week 9).
Name the encoding: UTF-8

A file stores bytes, not letters. An encoding is the rule that turns characters into bytes and back again. ASCII has English letters only. UTF-8 can store every Unicode character: one byte for each ASCII letter, two to four bytes for everything else. Nguyễn is 6 characters but 8 bytes, because ễ takes three. When the reader decodes those bytes with a different rule, the name comes back as nonsense such as Nguyá»…n, a mess with its own name: mojibake.

If you do not name an encoding, Java 8 and Python before 3.15 use the operating system’s default, and on Windows that is often not UTF-8. Java 18 (JEP 400) and Python 3.15 (PEP 686) switched their defaults to UTF-8, but Ed, your laptop and your marker’s computer may not all run the same version. So name it every time:

In 2010 Patrick McKenzie published Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names, a list of assumptions that real names break. media.lead: A visitors’ book only ever grows.
media.caption: Each visitor writes on the next empty line and nobody tears out the earlier pages: that is append mode, "a" in Python, new FileWriter(name, true) in Java. Write mode, "w", is a fresh book every time you open it: the old entries are gone before you write the first new word, even if you then write nothing. media.alt: A red pillar post box with a plate showing the last collection times
media.lead: Posted is not the same as delivered.
media.caption: Dropping a letter in the box feels finished, but it sits inside until the next collection, and the plate tells you when that is. A buffered writer is the box: println and write drop text in, flush() is an extra collection, and close() is the last collection before the box is locked. sections.title: Delimited records and quoting
concepts: A simple delimiter has a precondition

A delimiter is a character that means “this field ends here”. Splitting at it is safe exactly when it can never appear inside a value. That is a fact about your data, not about your code, so check it against real values before choosing:

DelimiterSafe when the values areBreaks on
comma ,numbers, codes, single-word namesAn, Mai; 1,000; 72,5 with a decimal comma
tabtext typed into a form fieldvalues pasted from a spreadsheet
semicolon ;numbers with a decimal commafree text
quoted CSVany text at allonly a reader that ignores the quoting rules

For a simple exercise it is fine to say “names contain no commas”, as long as you say it, in the contract. For real data, use a CSV writer and reader that understand quoting.

Java’s split drops empty fields at the end, and takes a pattern

"Linh,85,,".split(",") gives 2 strings in Java, because split throws away empty strings at the end; Python’s split(",") gives 4. Use split(",", -1) to keep them. And Java’s split takes a regular expression, where some characters are special: "a|b".split("|") splits between every character, and split(".") returns an empty array. Write split("\\|") or split("\\.").
Round-trip what you produce

The only proof that a format works is a round trip: write the data, read it back with the parser you intend to use, and compare the values, not just the number of lines. Count the records that went in and the records that came out, then check a few values field by field, especially the awkward ones.

Python’s csv.writer applies the quoting rules for you, quoting only the fields that need it, and csv.reader undoes them. Two details: the reader gives every field back as a str, so int(row[1]) is your job; and a real file for csv must be opened with newline="", because the documentation warns that otherwise newlines inside quoted fields are misread, and on Windows an extra \r is written. Java has no CSV parser in its standard library: write with a small quoting method like the one in Quote a field by hand below, and read general CSV with a library such as Apache Commons CSV or OpenCSV.

Nearly 16,000 missing test results, 2020

In October 2020, nearly 16,000 positive COVID-19 cases in England went unreported. Testing companies sent their results to Public Health England as CSV files, without problems. PHE then loaded them into Excel templates in the old .xls format, which holds only about 65,000 rows. Each test result used several rows, so each template could take about 1,400 cases, and when that total was reached, further cases were simply left off. No error appeared. Counting the records that went in and the records that came out is exactly the round-trip check that catches this. BBC News, 5 October 2020
The two quoting rules of CSV

Real CSV makes the round trip work for any text with two quoting rules, written down in RFC 4180. Rule 6: “Fields containing line breaks (CRLF), double quotes, and commas should be enclosed in double-quotes.” Rule 7: a double quote inside such a field is written twice.

ValueWritten asWhy
LinhLinhnothing special
An, Mai"An, Mai"contains a comma
Bao "Ben" Tran"Bao ""Ben"" Tran"contains a quote: wrap the field, double the quote
an address over two linesquoted, with the line break inside the quotescontains a line break
(empty)nothing between two commas: Linh,,85an empty field is still a field

“TCP implementations will follow a general principle of robustness: be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others.”

Jon Postel (editor), RFC 793, Transmission Control Protocol, 1981 Portrait: Carl Malamud · CC BY 2.0

Postel’s advice for network software is still quoted for files: be strict about what you write. Its second half is now debated: in 2023 the Internet Architecture Board published RFC 9413, noting that some interpretations of being liberal in what you accept “can negatively affect interoperability over time.” For this course: when your reader meets a line it does not understand, reject it with a clear message rather than guess (Week 9).
Named columns and CSV in both languages

Python can also name the columns. csv.DictWriter writes a header from a list of field names and then one row per dictionary; csv.DictReader reads the header and hands you each row as a dictionary, so row["mark"] still works if someone adds a column or swaps the order. In Java, read the header line yourself and look up each column’s position once, instead of hard-coding parts[1].

sections.title: Documents, summaries and repeatable tests
concepts: Choose a format that represents the structure

A line of CSV is flat: one record, a fixed list of fields. As soon as a record holds a list (all of a student’s marks) or another record (an address), you would have to invent a second delimiter, then a third. JSON already has the structure built in: objects with named fields, arrays, strings, numbers, true/false and null, nested as deep as you need.

A document that parses is not yet a valid report. {"name": "Linh"} is perfect JSON with no marks in it; {"marks": ["x"]} has a mark that is not a number. Check the fields you need, and their types and ranges, straight after parsing.

A JSON round trip can change your data

JSON object keys are always strings, so a Python dictionary with keys 1 and 2 comes back with keys "1" and "2". A tuple comes back as a list. Compare what you restore with what you saved, as the example A JSON round trip is not always the same data does.
JSON types in Python and Java

Each JSON type has a natural partner in Python; Java needs a library to do the mapping.

JSONPython after json.loadsJava
object {"name": "Linh"}dictwith a library: a Map or your own class
array [85, 90]lista List or an array
string "Linh"strString
number 85, 72.5int, floatint, double
true, false, nullTrue, False, Nonetrue, false, null

Python’s json module is in the standard library; Java SE has no JSON parser, so real Java projects add a library such as Jackson or Gson. Three json.dumps options are worth knowing: indent=2 for people, sort_keys=True so the same data always gives the same text, and ensure_ascii=False to keep Nguyễn readable instead of Nguy\u1ec5n. Since RFC 8259 (2017), JSON exchanged between systems “MUST be encoded using UTF-8”.

Choosing the shape of the data first makes the code that reads it simpler, an old observation about programs that holds just as well for files:
Test a pipeline in layers

A report program is a pipeline of layers: calculate the totals, format the record, write it, read it back. Test each layer on its own, so a failure tells you where to look, like the stack of sieves in the photo.

A test needs output that is repeatable: the same input must give the same characters on every run and every computer. Keep out anything that changes by itself: the current time, random numbers, the iteration order of a Java HashMap or a Python set of strings, and the computer’s locale. Sort before you print, pass Locale.ROOT, use sort_keys=True.

Then compare the whole text. “It ran without an exception” is not a test: it passes with the wrong mode, a missing newline or the columns swapped. Write the report into a StringWriter or StringIO, compare it with the exact string you expect, and print repr of the difference when it fails, so invisible characters show up. The example Test the report, not the screen does this.

One test with a real file, the rest in memory

Memory streams make tests fast and repeatable. Keep one test that really writes a file on Ed and reads it back: it is the only one that checks the working directory, the file mode and the encoding.
A test list for a report

Pick test inputs that are most likely to expose a bug, not the ones most likely to pass. For a marks report:

Test inputWhy this oneExpected
[85, 49, 50]ordinary data, including the boundarycount 3, passed 2
[50]exactly on the pass markpassed 1, not 0
[]no data at allthe header and 0,0, or the error your contract chose
a name with a comma or a quotequotingthe same name after a round trip
a last line without \nthe reader’s edge casethe record is still read
the program run twicethe file modeone copy with "w", two with "a"

To prove that the eventual disk is writable and its file permissions are correct.
To prevent the report formatter from ever producing an invalid record or delimiter.
To make every reader interpret a comma inside a name as ordinary unquoted text.
quiz.why: A memory writer isolates formatting; a separate integration check covers the file destination.

quiz.q: A JSON document parses successfully. What remains to check?
opts: Nothing at all, because parsing proves every required field and allowed mark is present.
Whether its structure and values meet the application rules.
Only its indentation, because JSON parsers guarantee that field meanings are correct.
Only its filename extension, because the document contents cannot affect a program.
quiz.why: Syntax validity and domain validity are separate checks.

misc.title: Two characters for one new line
misc.html:
M2.1A typewriter with two jobs

On a mechanical teleprinter such as the Teletype Model 33 (the machine in the Section 1 photo), starting a new line was two separate movements: carriage return moved the print head back to the left edge, and line feed rolled the paper up one line. ASCII gave each its own code: CR is 13 ( ) and LF is 10 ( ). The return was the slow part, so CR was sent first, and the head could still be travelling when the next character arrived; machines were often sent extra padding characters to give it time.

Operating systems then split into three camps, and they never fully reunited:

CR LF

Two characters, like the teleprinter

Early systems that drove a Teletype directly stored both codes in their files. Most of DEC’s minicomputer systems used CR LF, so did CP/M and MS-DOS, and Windows still does.

LF

One character, translated on the way out

Multics, begun in 1964, stored only LF and let a device driver send whatever the printer needed. Unix followed Multics, and so do Linux and macOS today.

CR

The odd one out

The Apple II and classic Mac OS used CR alone. Mac OS X, built on Unix, switched to LF.

2018

Notepad learns LF

Windows Notepad showed a Unix file as one long line until Microsoft added support for LF and CR line endings in 2018 (Microsoft announcement).

Source for this history: Wikipedia, “Newline”, History and Representation.
